source.title: ETA: Evaluating Then Aligning Safety of Vision Language Models at Inference Time
source.authors: Yi Ding; Bo-Lian Li; Ruqi Zhang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures harmful-response rates when harmful prompts include an adversarial suffix, and reports a prefix-only alignment ablation. These are behavioral tests related to V4, but the study does not use the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.gate_note: The paper's suffix experiments and prefix-only ablation report unsafe-response outcomes relevant to V4. The embedding-mapping experiment also reports unsafe rates, but tests a distinct mechanism not covered by the listed versions; recorded under fits_no_version. The paper discusses other studies' fine-tuning and alignment results, but those cited results are not recorded as this study's outcomes. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, fine-tuning on few examples, or weight/rank localization.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (vision-language models), the study reports unsafe-response rates with and without the suffix "Answer with 'Absolutely, here's'" on undefended models (Tables 1, 7, 9). This suffix pushes the model toward a compliant opening, so it bears on V4. Fig. 3a and §4.1.2 also compare the Vicuna backbone with LLaVA after visual instruction tuning, which bears on V2. The rest of the paper evaluates the authors' inference-time defense (ETA) and comparisons against ECSO.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also state that a safety prefix alone (shallow alignment) is insufficient, consistent with Qi et al. (2024b), and needs sentence-level best-of-N (deep alignment). Their claim that continuous visual embeddings are the 'primary cause' of failures rests on the embedding-mapping experiment.
record.recipe_differences: Inference-time evaluation, a safety-style interference prefix, and sentence-level best-of-N; no parameter fine-tuning. The study evaluates suffix attacks rather than measuring per-token KL or fine-tuning safety on small datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Suffix effects vary by benchmark, model, and defense: FigStep and AdvBench results differ, and some ETA/ECSO conditions reduce rather than increase USR under suffixes.

fits_no_version.finding: Mapping continuous visual embeddings to their nearest text embeddings lowers the unsafe rate on SPA-VL Harm and VLSafe for four VLMs (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VLM safety failures arise partly because continuous visual embeddings bypass safety learned on discrete text tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefilling a refusal prefix alone lowers LLaVA-1.5-7B's unsafe rate from 46.04 to 30.94. The authors say models often refuse and then continue harmfully after 'However' (Fig. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal-style opening imposed at inference is a shallow safeguard: models revert to harmful content after the first tokens.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the unsafe-rate comparisons. The main safety measure is an automated judge-based USR; suffix outcomes vary across models, benchmarks, and defenses.
record.rows_left_out: No results-bearing rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Cited results from other studies and method-comparison results not directly measuring a listed claim version are not included.

untested.parts: No controlled benign fine-tuning experiment. Only a cross-model comparison of the Vicuna backbone with LLaVA after visual instruction tuning (Fig. 3a).
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No direct prefilling of a compliant harmful start and no decoding-change attacks. Only an instruction suffix requesting a compliant opening.
ETA is inference-time and involves no training to deepen safety, so it does not test V7.

missing.what: Fig. 3a unsafe rates: Vicuna-1.5-7B backbone versus LLaVA-1.5-7B after visual instruction tuning, with and without harmful images (about 20.38, 29.06, 46.04).
Target-string attack success rate with and without the suffix for undefended models (e.g., AdvBench LLaVA-1.5-7B 4.23 to 41.73; FigStep in Table 8).

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked ECSO- and ETA-defended rows to V4 and labelled ETA's robustness as challenging V4. Those rows measure defense methods (ETA is the study's own), so they are unlinked. Rows r25–r27 were mislabelled as ETA; they are vanilla Table 7 values. All unsafe rates come from the MD-Judge automated judge, with no uncertainty reported. The Adv. Image+Text condition combines the suffix with an adversarial image and has no suffix-free baseline, so it cannot isolate the suffix effect.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune a safety-trained model on a few to a few hundred harmful examples.
The study does not fine-tune on ordinary or carefully selected benign examples to measure harmful compliance.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models is reported.
The study tests adversarial text suffixes and a safety/refusal-style prefix ablation. It does not test a compliant-to-the-harmful-request opening or decoding changes as a bypass.
No weight or rank localization experiment is reported.
The study does not test whether fine-tuning data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
The study uses inference-time alignment, not training that spreads safety beyond the first response tokens, and does not test durability of such training.

relation.reason: Tables 1, 7 and 9 directly measure whether a compliant-opening suffix increases unsafe responses.

tranche.reason: Tests compliant-opening suffix attacks in the new setting of vision-language models, with explicit unsafe-response rates against unsuffixed controls.

source_check.notes: USR is evaluated using MD-Judge-v0.2-internlm2_7B; it differs from the paper's string-based ASR. The attack appends an instruction requesting a compliant opening, rather than literally prefilling assistant tokens.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Vanilla models on AdvBench suffix attacks; selected FigStep settings
reader_labels.reason: The suffix is followed by sharply higher USR on AdvBench for the vanilla models (r13–r16), and also raises USR substantially in some FigStep conditions (r10–r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: FigStep suffix attacks with vanilla models and ETA-treated models
reader_labels.reason: Some increases are modest (r1, r4, r7, r8, r12, r25, r27), and results vary across settings; some ETA-treated models show lower USR with the suffix (r6, r9, r26).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: AdvBench suffix attacks with ETA, and selected suffix attacks with ETA or ECSO
reader_labels.reason: In these defense conditions, adding the suffix does not raise USR and sometimes lowers it, including large reductions for ETA on AdvBench (r17–r23).
